discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Mild day today with a warm front to the north and a cold front still offshore. Cold front moving through tonight bringing rain and windy conditions to most of the area along with high surf to the beaches. Post frontal showers ending Sunday. Another wet and windy system moving into the area Monday night but not nearly as strong as the system tonight. Atmospheric river settling up over Western Washington Tuesday will lift north Tuesday night. Cold front stalling near the coast Wednesday and Thursday moving through Thursday night. Another system will arrive Friday.
hydrology: River flooding is not expected through the next seven days. Multiple weather systems moving through the area in the next week. While current precipitation forecasts are not expected to cause flooding, this will saturate soils and raise base flows that could bring a concern with storm systems by late next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Mild day today with a warm front to the north and a cold front still offshore. Cold front moving through tonight bringing rain and windy conditions to most of the area along with high surf to the beaches. Post frontal showers ending Sunday. Another wet and windy system moving into the area Monday night but not nearly as strong as the system tonight. Atmospheric river settling up over Western Washington Tuesday will lift north Tuesday night. Cold front stalling near the coast Wednesday and Thursday moving through Thursday night. Another system will arrive Friday.

sections.title: Short term (today through Monday)
paragraphs: Western Washington remaining in the warm sector today with a warm front to the north and a cold front still offshore late this afternoon. Rain developing along the coast this afternoon with the rain not making it as far east as the Puget Sound by late afternoon. Highs near 60.

Cold front reaching the coast this evening. The front will move through the Puget Sound area around midnight and will be into the Cascades by early Sunday morning. This front has some punch to it. Model 925 mb winds just ahead, with and just behind the front in the 55 to 65 knot range along the coast and in the 35 to 50 knot range over the interior from the Puget Sound northward. Some of these winds will mix down to the surface. Have upgraded the high wind watch on the beaches to a high wind warning beginning late this afternoon with southerly wind gusts has high as 60 mph. Have added wind advisories for the interior coast zones, along the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Admiralty Inlet, and over the interior near the Puget Sound from Seattle Northward including the San Juan Islands for southerly wind gusts 45 to 50 mph tonight into early Sunday morning. Strongest winds will be with the frontal passage this evening along the coast and around midnight for the interior. Our benign October weather left plenty of leaves on the trees increasing the chances for impacts with borderline advisory wind speeds.

In addition to the winds, seas will rise rapidly into the 22 to 26 foot range along the ocean beaches tonight. A high surf warning has replaced the high surf advisory with the warning beginning at 10 pm. Seas will be well above 10 feet by low tide late this afternoon at Mocrocks beach. This along with strong winds will make for dangerous conditions for the clam dig.

Weather calming down Sunday, although breezy conditions will still be present in the morning. Post frontal shower activity will be minimal with most of the activity over with by noon. Highs in the mid 50s under mostly cloudy skies. Seas remaining elevated in the 22 to 26 foot range.

Break in the weather continuing Sunday night with the next system near 135W by 12Z Monday. The front is showing signs of becoming negatively tilted with the parent low moving north along 142W near 55W early in the morning. Lows in the mid 30s to mid 40s. Seas easing overnight. The high surf warning will come to an end at 10 pm Sunday evening.

Front moving east Monday but still offshore by late Monday afternoon. Rain reaching the coast in the afternoon with a chance of rain inland by late afternoon. Parent surface low way up in the Gulf of Alaska. Model 925 mb winds 30 to 40 knots along the coast with the front and weaker inland. This system will not produce winds like the system tonight. Felton

sections.title: Long term (Monday night through Friday)
paragraphs: Models in good agreement with the front moving through Monday night and another front right on its heels for Tuesday. Atmospheric river setting up Tuesday night with the bulk of the moisture aimed at Vancouver Island. Warm front hanging over Western Washington. Model solutions becoming inconsistent Wednesday as an upper level trough digs south offshore. This will push the warm front north into British Columbia. Solutions for the trailing cold front range from stalling along the coast to stalling back near 130W Wednesday. Inconsistencies continue Thursday with solutions split between what is left of the front moving through to the front remaining stalled off the coast. There is better agreement Friday with another system moving across the Pacific into the area. In general chance pops for Wednesday and Thursday with rain along the coast and rain likely inland Friday.

Mild temperatures through the period. Highs near 60 Tuesday and Thursday, lower to mid 60s Wednesday, then back down to the mid 50s with the rain Friday. Highs Wednesday will be close to records in some locations. Record high for Seattle is 65 set in 1990. Current forecast high is 64. Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: West to southwest flow aloft will increase this morning and become strong this afternoon and evening as a vigorous frontal system moves onshore into the region. Plentiful low level moisture and light surface winds have resulted in a mixed bag of ceilings this morning from LIFR to MVFR for most areas along with areas of surface visibility below 3 statute miles. The low ceilings and reduced visibility are expected to scour out for most areas by 18Z-20Z as low level east to southeasterly flow begins to increase ahead of the incoming system. Ceilings are expected to deteriorate back to MVFR in increasing rain along the coast after 00Z. Rain will spread to most of the interior by 06Z with ceilings near or just above 3000 feet. Strong southerly surface winds with gusts 35 to 45 knots will develop along the coast late this afternoon/evening with strong winds spreading to interior areas this evening and overnight.

KSEA...VFR ceilings persist at the terminal this morning, with lower clouds within the vicinity not expected to push into the terminal. Gusty surface winds will develop by late this afternoon and increase through the evening. Rain is expected to arrive between 04-06Z with ceilings lowering to near or just above 3000 feet. Surface winds light E/SE this morning will rise to 8 to 12 knots this afternoon then quickly increase to southerly 15 to 25 knots gusting to 30 to 35 knots this evening and persisting overnight before gradually easing Sunday morning. Low level wind shear is expected just ahead of and with the front this evening with 2000 foot winds becoming southerly at 45 to 50 knots.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: An active weather pattern will continue into next week as a series of frontal systems impact area waters. A vigorous frontal system associated with 970 millibar surface low curling northeastward offshore tonight is expected to produce a period of storm force wind gusts over the coastal waters later today into tonight with gales across the remainder of the waters tonight. Seas will build to 21 to 28 feet late tonight into Sunday before gradually subsiding Sunday night into Monday. Weak high pressure will briefly build over the waters on Monday before another deepening surface low moving toward Haida Gwaii pushes a front across the waters Monday night into Tuesday.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: River flooding is not expected through the next seven days. Multiple weather systems moving through the area in the next week. While current precipitation forecasts are not expected to cause flooding, this will saturate soils and raise base flows that could bring a concern with storm systems by late next week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active weather pattern will continue into next week and produce periods of rain and windy conditions, particularly along the coast. A large westerly swell will bring high surf Sunday and an elevated threat of sneaker waves through the weekend.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active weather pattern will continue into next week and produce periods of rain and windy conditions, particularly along the coast. A large westerly swell will bring high surf Sunday and an elevated threat of sneaker waves through the weekend.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Our latest upper-level shortwave trough and accompanying frontal boundary are pushing eastward tonight with lingering showers rapidly decreasing and tapering off. This is followed by increasing upper-level heights Saturday morning as the overall longwave pattern amplifies due in part to a strengthening low over the eastern Pacific - thisll come in play late in the day. In the mean time, much of Saturday ends up fairly pleasant for early November, especially across the interior valleys. Thanks to the warm southerly flow aloft, daytime temperatures should jump into the mid 60s along the I-5 corridor as winds help to mix out fog and low clouds present early this morning.

Our attention shifts to another weather system that will push a stronger front eastward into the region late this afternoon and evening. As far as these impacts are concerned, the latest NBM guidance still has a 40-50% chance for wind gusts of 58 mph or greater along the coast, and the REFS guidance has probabilities of 60-70% along coastal beaches and headlands. The overall set-up appears to support these probabilities as well, 925mb winds (~1800ft) right along the coast maxing out around 55-65 knots along the frontal boundary. Without a notable temperature inversion to keep these winds pinned above the surface, heavier precipitation and more convective elements along the the front will definitely have an opportunity to mix towards the surface. Winds along the coast likely ramp up Saturday afternoon with the highest gusts along the coast likely occurring between 4-8PM.

Winds also increase across the interior lowlands Saturday evening and overnight, albeit they will not be nearly as strong as the coast. Both the latest NBM and REFS guidance indicate there is a 20-30% chance along the I-5 corridor for peak wind gusts above 40 mph Saturday evening, which would produce at least isolated down tree limbs and power outages. The majority of wind gusts will likely be in the 20-35 mph range, though.

Rainfall totals with this late Saturday storm system do not appear concerning for river flooding given the quick moving nature of the front. Confidence is high the region breaks to showers the second half of Saturday night into Sunday morning, followed by showers ending near sunset Sunday evening. That said, there is a signal among the high resolution model guidance for a narrow cold frontal rain band to materialize Saturday evening, but at this point, it still only appears there is a 10-20% chance for hourly rainfall totals exceeding a 0.25" per hour Saturday evening at any given location along the Interstate 5 corridor. With that said, REFS guidance suggests the probabilities are above 50% for the Salem area specifically. Either way, this hourly rainfall rate is typically what is needed to produce nuisance urban flooding in the October- December timeframe when deciduous trees are dropping their leaves and storm drains clog easily. Once showers end Sunday evening dry weather returns overnight with patchy fog across the inland valleys.

Looking at next week, ensembles are in agreement that the progressive pattern will continue, but there is relatively high uncertainty in the details. Global ensembles are in strong agreement with over 90% of the membership suggesting the next storm system arrives late Monday or Tuesday. The majority of the global ensemble membership also suggest rainfall amounts that will be beneficial. The probability we see rainfall amounts exceed 2.5-3 inches in a 24-hour period across even the higher terrain appears less than 5-10%.

While there is general agreement shortwave ridging will temporarily build across the region Wednesday into Thursday, there is a still a sizable chunk of the global ensembles that suggest a shortwave trough offshore will place an elongated SSW->NNE oriented atmospheric river close enough to the coast that it will continue rain there during this period. Nonetheless, the majority of the global ensemble guidance suggests this atmospheric river will remain offshore and be directed farther north towards the Olympic Peninsula and Vancouver Island with the region ultimately getting a reprieve from the rain.

All three ensemble systems are in broad agreement another storm system will bring rain and wind to the region late next week or next weekend. Fortunately, any signs of an overly impactful wind or rain event in the global ensembles is still relatively low (10-20% chance or less) at this point, though will need to keep an eye on flooding concerns depending on the strength of these weather systems as soils become more saturated from multiple rounds of rain.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 18Z Sunday...Satellite imagery and terminal observations as of late Saturday morning depicts a mix of of LIFR, IFR, MVFR, and VFR conditions across the region along with high clouds ahead of the next system. The coast remains predominately MVFR, while terminals across the Willamette Valley are gradually clearing out of the fog and low stratus from early this morning. KUAO and KSLE remain LIFR, however, expect improving conditions to VFR by 19-20z Sat.

Tonight, a cold front will push through the region, returning rain and a brief period of IFR/MVFR CIGs and VIS. Expect these lower CIGs and VIS between 02-05z Sun along the coast, and 05-08z Sun across the Valley during the frontal passage. Behind the front, conditions will quickly improve as rain transitions into showers and CIGs improve to a mix of MVFR/VFR. Winds generally under 10 kt across the area through 21z Sat. After 21z Sat-00z Sun, will see southerly winds gradually increasing ahead of the front. Tonight, expect southerly wind gusts to peak around 35-40 kt along the coast, and 20- 25 kt across the Valley.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Expect predominately VFR conditions with high clouds through the early evening. Tonight after 04-05z Sun, the next front will push through and return moderate to locally heavy rain along with IFR/MVFR CIGs and VIS through 07-09z Sun. Conditions improve to VFR behind the front with showers. Southerly winds increase after 00z Sun with gusts up to 25 kt through late tonight. Winds gradually decrease after 08-10z Sun.   -10

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: An active weather pattern will continue across the waters into next week. A persistent westerly swell will maintain steep and hazardous seas of 14 to 17 ft through Saturday morning. Therefore, a Hazardous Seas Warning remains in effect through 10 AM Sat across all waters including the Columbia River Bar.

The next stronger front moves eastward across the waters Saturday afternoon and evening. There is high confidence (>90% chance) for high-end gale force wind gusts of 40-45 kt across the waters south of Cape Foulweather with an 80-90% chance for at least a brief period of Storm Force wind gusts of 50-55 kt across the waters north of Cape Foulweather. The strongest winds will most likely occur across the waters off the Columbia River mouth. Winds appear most likely to peak across the northern outer waters between 1500-1800 and 1700-2000 for our inner waters. Gusty west winds will persist across our northern outer waters well into Saturday night.

A large westerly swell will then push into the waters early Sunday morning with high confidence for seas climbing above 20 ft for a 12-18 hour stretch. At this point, it appears seas will likely reach 20 ft between 0200-0500 on Sunday and not drop below 20 ft until 1800-2100 on Sunday. Latest guidance continues to suggest seas peak around 24-25 ft across the northern waters and 21-22 ft across the southern waters. Hedged towards seas peaking a couple feet higher than this in the official forecast given the pattern.

Seas gradually subside Sunday night into Monday. Additional storm systems will bring additional rounds of Gale Force winds to the waters with seas generally hovering between 10-20 ft for much of next week. The next round of Gale Force winds appears most likely (80% chance) to arrive late Monday into Tuesday.

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A westerly swell of 13-15 ft at 14-15 seconds today will bring a high threat of sneaker waves along the coast. A much larger westerly swell arrives overnight and builds Sunday morning peaking somewhere between 20-30 ft with a dominant period of 16 seconds midday Sunday. This will result in beach erosion and bring an even higher threat of sneaker waves along the coast on Sunday. Extreme caution should be used if you plan to visit beaches on Sunday. The large wave runup will dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically caught unsuspecting people and killed or seriously enjoyed them so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave. Given the momentum behind these large longer period waves, it's not out of the question that we receive a report or two of damage to infrastructure along the coast, particularly around high tide midday Sunday.
